newsitem.title: ITALY: Italian govt poised to pass budget amid criticism.
newsitem.headline: Italian govt poised to pass budget amid criticism.

text.p: Prime Minister Romano Prodi's cabinet met on Thursday to approve a mini-budget amid widespread criticism that it would only be a stop-gap attempt to win Italy entry to the single European currency.

The government is expected to introduce a package designed to cut around 15.3 trillion lire ($9.1 billion) off this year's deficit in a last gasp bid to plug a hole in state accounts and meet the terms of the Maastricht Treaty.
Media leaks said companies would bear the brunt of the budget and be forced to stump up some six trillion lire in the form of advance taxes on severance payment funds.
"The measures that are about to be proposed are not only useless...but actually counter-productive," newspaper Il Corriere della Sera said in a hard-hitting editorial.

The Treasury is expected to raise more money by delaying payment of severance handouts to state workers taking retirement, by introducing a tax amnesty on unpaid social security contributions and by cutting some spending plans.
When Prodi announced that more belt-tightening would be needed earlier this year, he pledged that the package would be based on structural reforms.

But faced by strong opposition from political ally the hardleft Communist Refoundation, he had to renounce plans for an assault on Italy's outdated welfare system, while the sluggish economy prevented any new tax hikes.
"This corrective package...mirrors the fragility of the coalition and the difficulty of operating on an economic body as weak and weatherbeaten as ours," La Stampa daily said.
Financial markets reacted cautiously to the budget, relieved that the centre-left coalition had agreed on a package, but dissapointed by the contents.
"The government is making enormous efforts but the problem is that they're not making structural changes," said Ken Wattret economist with Paris in London.

Many commentators believed that the government might succeed in reducing Italy's deficit to three percent of gross domestic product (GDP) as demanded by Maastricht, but added that the Treasury was storing up trouble for itself in the process.

"Perhaps the budget will satisfy the Maastricht criteria, but it is basically inadequate to resolve the problems of our country's public finances," top selling financial daily Il Sole 24 Ore wrote in an editorial.
Corriere della Sera thought Italy's European Union partners would baulk at the package.

"The Germans will renounce the single currency rather than share it with a country that might artificially get its deficit to the three percent level but has not found the political consensus needed to resolve long-term problems..." it said.

The centre-right opposition bloc, led by Silvio Berlusconi, had called on the government to cut welfare spending in its mini-budget and economists said this was the only way to secure lasting peace for the heavily indebted economy.
While sidestepping the hugely controversial issue in the corrective budget, Prodi is expected to launch a thorough overview of social spending before the summer.
"It seems there is wide agreement on the need for this," cabinet secretary Enrico Micheli said on Wednesday.

But with Prodi's supporters covering every political shade from the Marxist Refoundation to the free-market Italian Renewal party, headed by Foreign Minister Lamberto Dini, an agreement is likely to take months to hammer out.
